newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communists hate new Russian minister Chubais.
newsitem.headline: Communists hate new Russian minister Chubais.

text.p: Anatoly Chubais, the liberal thrust from the Kremlin staff to number two in the government on Thursday, is despised by communists who dubbed him public enemy number one for spearheading Russia's privatisation campaign.

The 41-year-old economist's move from Kremlin chief-of-staff to first deputy to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is a big vote of confidence by President Boris Yeltsin in the man who, more than any other, got him re-elected.

But the tall, fair-haired Chubais, who ran the campaign that brought Yeltsin back from the verge of political extinction, is hated by communists and nationalists and faces a hard time from the parliament, where they call the shots.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, whom Yeltsin beat last July after a hectic campaign that helped provoke the heart trouble from which he is only now recovering, denounced Chubais as the leader of a "fifth column" of Western interests.
"Is is a challenge to the whole of Russia," Gennady Seleznyov, communist speaker of the State Duma lower house of parliament, told Interfax news agency on Friday.
Chubais is admired by the International Monetary Fund and the Group of Seven industrial nations for his strong grasp of Western economic ideas and his fluent English.

Now charged by Yeltsin with cleaning up an economy in which business and politics have become hopelessly entangled with each other and with organised crime, Chubais himself is accused by the opposition of lining his own pockets.

Communist legislators have twice sent motions to Yeltsin urging him to sack Chubais for corruption and earning a private income while in the state's employ. At one stage this year they circulated copies of Chubais's credit card bills.

The Kremlin chief-of-staff, who has a taste for sharp western suits and foreign travel, has consistently denied all the charges, saying he owes what wealth he has to lecturing abroad during the period he was out of government.
His new job completes an impressive comeback for the St. Petersburg intellectual after he was removed in January 1996 as first deputy premier in charge of economic reforms.

Yeltsin sacrificed Chubais in the wake of sweeping communist gains in the December 1995 parliamentary elections. The president said that if Chubais, who first entered the reformist government of Yegor Gaidar in 1991, had gone earlier, then the government party would have doubled its share of the vote.
Any hard feelings were apparently forgotten, however, when Yeltsin appointed Chubais to head the presidential administration after he won a new four-year term.

With Yeltsin crippled by heart trouble shortly before his victory, Chubais was to play a crucial role. He was caught up in manouevring for power that was sparked by doubts over whether Yeltsin could continue in office.
Kremlin security chief Alexander Lebed was sacked in October after Yeltsin, probably primed by Chubais, accused him of plotting a coup.
The chief-of-staff seemed to reach a modus vivendi with Chernomyrdin, who as Yeltsin's constitutional deputy, stood in for the president during his heart bypass operation in November.

Some analysts suggest Chubais's new role behind Chernomyrdin could set the younger man up for the premiership if the 58-year-old prime minister succeeds Yeltsin in three years' time. Chubais is thought to be too young and have too many enemies to harbour his own presidential ambitions -- yet.
Chubais is married. He has a son and a daughter from a previous marriage.
